origin: Original workshop built by Muse (AI assistant) on 19 November 2026 at Steven Powell's direction, from his proposal in the Everyday Cool ideas side chat that morning: the metric system for Americans, compared with US customary units — converters, examples, STEM articles, weight and volume comparison tools — with the banner art direction in his words: a robot with scales and a chart behind it showing what each prefix means. He chose the name 'Everyday Measure' from the options offered. The room carries an interactive prefix ladder (mega through nano plus the base unit, each prefix with its plain-words meaning and a climb-the-ladder bench), four converter benches that show their working from the exact legal definitions published by NIST (1 in = 2.54 cm, 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg, 1 US gallon = 3.785411784 L, all exact by definition), seven feel-it anchor cards labelled exact or approximate, a comparison shelf reading six familiar things in both systems at once (second reading computed by the same converters, approximate things marked), three trap cards (tonne/US ton/long ton; US vs Imperial gallon; fluid ounce vs ounce), the Mars Climate Orbiter and Gimli Glider breakage stories, a short honest history (1790s France, Treaty of the Meter 1875, Mendenhall Order 1893, the 1959 exact inch and pound, the voluntary Metric Conversion Act 1975), and a seven-link verified shelf (NIST SI Units, NIST SP 811, four Wikipedia articles, Khan Academy with its script-challenge noted). The banner's first generation was rejected for a garbled staircase (DECI duplicated, DEKA and HECTO swapped) and regenerated with the step order spelled out; the shipped banner reads KILO, HECTO, DEKA, METRE, DECI, CENTI, MILLI correctly. It enters the catalog under 'Science,' immediately after Everyday Body. This folder is the maintained original.
